rooms.title: DPDP Overview and Scope
learning_objectives: Read the Act's commencement mechanism.
Identify the core scope of the Act.
Distinguish digital personal data processing inside India from qualifying processing outside India.
Use exact statutory definitions instead of invented categories.

tasks.title: Task 1: Commencement and definitions
official_text:
1. (1) This Act may be called the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

(2) It shall come into force on such date as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint and different dates may be appointed for different provisions of this Act and any reference in any such provision to the commencement of this Act shall be construed as a reference to the coming into force of that provision.
tasks.simple_words: Section 1 creates a commencement mechanism where different provisions can start on different dates. Section 2 supplies the Act's own vocabulary. In this room, use those definitions exactly as the legal anchor.
key_terms: person determining purpose and means of processing personal data
individual to whom personal data relates, with specified guardian treatment
person processing personal data on behalf of a Data Fiduciary
tasks.real_world_example: A university stores a student's name, email and admission record in a digital ERP. The Act's definitions determine which statutory terms describe the actors and data before any compliance conclusion is drawn.
tasks.student_angle: A college ERP vendor hosts student records. The college determines why the records are used, while the vendor processes them on the college's behalf. Identify the roles from Section 2 instead of using GDPR terminology.
common_mistakes: Every data item is automatically digital personal data.
The definition in Section 2(n) is personal data in digital form.
Data Processor means the organisation that decides why data is processed.
Section 2(k) defines a Data Processor as processing personal data on behalf of a Data Fiduciary.

questions.prompt: Under Section 1(2), who appoints the commencement date(s)?
options: The Central Government by notification in the Official Gazette
The Data Protection Board
Every Data Fiduciary
The Appellate Tribunal
questions.why: Section 1(2) expressly assigns appointment of commencement date(s) to the Central Government by notification in the Official Gazette.
why_wrong: The Act assigns the notification function to the Central Government, not the Board.
The Board is not given this power by Section 1(2).
A private Data Fiduciary has no statutory power to appoint commencement dates.

questions.prompt: Section 1(2) allows different dates for different provisions of the Act.
options: True
False
questions.why: The provision expressly says different dates may be appointed for different provisions.
why_wrong: False is incorrect because the provision expressly permits different dates.

why_wrong: Data Principal is the individual to whom personal data relates.
Data Processor processes personal data on behalf of a Data Fiduciary.

options: Data Processor

questions.why: Section 2(k) gives this exact definition.
why_wrong: Data Principal is the individual to whom the data relates.

why_wrong: Section 3 concerns application of the Act.

options: Data Fiduciary

why_wrong: Section 2(i) defines Data Fiduciary.
Section 2(k) defines Data Processor.

tasks.title: Task 2: Application of the Act
official_text:
3. Subject to the provisions of this Act, it shall—
(a) apply to the processing of digital personal data within the territory of India where the personal data is collected—
(i) in digital form; or
(ii) in non-digital form and digitised subsequently;
(b) also apply to processing of digital personal data outside the territory of India, if such processing is in connection with any activity related to offering of goods or services to Data Principals within the territory of India;
(c) not apply to—
(i) personal data processed by an individual for any personal or domestic purpose; and
(ii) personal data that is made or caused to be made publicly available by—
(A) the Data Principal to whom such personal data relates; or
(B) any other person who is under an obligation under any law for the time being in force in India to make such personal data publicly available.

Illustration.
X, an individual, while blogging her views, has publicly made available her personal data on social media. In such case, the provisions of this Act shall not apply.
tasks.simple_words: Section 3 sets the geographic and activity scope, then lists exclusions. It covers specified digital personal data processing inside India and can also cover qualifying processing outside India connected with offering goods or services to Data Principals in India.
key_terms: the operations listed in Section 2(x) performed on digital personal data
individual to whom personal data relates
tasks.real_world_example: An overseas edtech platform offers a paid course to Data Principals in India and processes their digital personal data outside India. Section 3(b) is the provision to examine for territorial scope.
tasks.student_angle: A student posts their own phone number publicly on a social profile. Section 3(c)(ii)(A) is the specific exclusion to examine for data made publicly available by the Data Principal.
common_mistakes: Section 3 applies to every kind of personal data anywhere in the world.
Section 3 has specific scope conditions and exclusions.
Any foreign processing is automatically outside the Act.
Section 3(b) expressly addresses certain processing outside India.

options: Section 3(a)
Section 3(b)
Section 3(c)(i)
Section 15
questions.why: Section 3(b) expressly addresses that situation.
why_wrong: Section 3(a) concerns processing within India.
Section 3(c)(i) is a personal/domestic exclusion.
Section 15 concerns duties of Data Principals.

questions.prompt: Section 3(c)(i) excludes personal data processed by an individual for a personal or domestic purpose.
options: True
False
questions.why: That is the express text of Section 3(c)(i).
why_wrong: False contradicts the express exclusion.

questions.prompt: An overseas service offers goods to Data Principals in India and processes their digital personal data outside India. Which provision should the learner inspect first?
options: Section 3(b)
Section 2(f)
Section 15
Section 33
questions.why: Section 3(b) directly addresses qualifying processing outside India connected with offering goods or services to Data Principals in India.
why_wrong: Section 2(f) is the definition of child.
Section 15 is a duty of Data Principal.
Section 33 concerns penalties.

questions.prompt: Which is expressly excluded by Section 3(c)(ii)(A)?
options: Data made publicly available by the Data Principal
All data held by companies
All data processed outside India
All data in non-digital form
questions.why: Section 3(c)(ii)(A) names personal data made or caused to be made publicly available by the Data Principal.
why_wrong: The other options are not the exclusion stated in Section 3(c)(ii)(A).

questions.prompt: Fill the flag with the section that contains the Act's application and exclusions.
options: DPDP{section_3}
DPDP{section_4}
DPDP{section_7}
DPDP{section_11}
questions.why: Section 3 is titled Application of Act.
why_wrong: Section 4 covers grounds for processing; Section 7 certain legitimate uses; Section 11 access rights.

rooms.summary: Section 1 establishes phased commencement. Section 2 supplies statutory definitions. Section 3 defines the Act's application and exclusions. Do not extend these provisions beyond the words in the source.
cheat_sheet: Section 1: commencement by Central Government notification; different dates may apply.
Section 3: scope inside India, specified qualifying processing outside India, and stated exclusions.

final_challenge.scenario: A foreign edtech platform processes digital personal data outside India while offering services to Data Principals in India. The student must identify the provision governing the territorial application before making any further conclusion.
final_challenge.answer_explanation: The scenario directly tracks Section 3(b).

tasks.title: Task 1: Actors

key_terms: registered person enabling consent management through an accessible, transparent and interoperable platform
individual to whom personal data relates
processes on behalf of Data Fiduciary

common_mistakes: A Data Processor is always the person deciding the purpose.
Section 2(k) ties the Processor to processing on behalf of a Data Fiduciary.
Consent Manager and Data Fiduciary are interchangeable terms.

tasks.title: Task 2: Data terms
tasks.simple_words: The Act defines the data category, breach category and processing activity itself. Processing is broad and includes listed operations such as collection, storage, use, sharing and erasure.
key_terms: listed unauthorised or accidental events compromising confidentiality, integrity or availability
wholly or partly automated operation or set of operations performed on digital personal data
tasks.real_world_example: A learning app stores a student's account information, retrieves it to display a profile, and later erases it. Those operations fall within the Act's definition of processing when its conditions are met.

common_mistakes: Section 2(x) lists many operations beyond collection.

rooms.title: Notice and Consent
learning_objectives: Identify what Section 5 requires in a consent request notice.
Identify the statutory properties of consent in Section 6.
Connect Rule 3 to the Act's notice requirement without adding unsupported requirements.

tasks.title: Task 1: Notice
official_text:
5. (1) Every request made to a Data Principal under section 6 for consent shall be accompanied or preceded by a notice given by the Data Fiduciary to the Data Principal, informing her,—
(i) the personal data and the purpose for which the same is proposed to be processed;
(ii) the manner in which she may exercise her rights under sub-section (4) of section 6 and section 13; and
(iii) the manner in which the Data Principal may make a complaint to the Board, in such manner and as may be prescribed.

Illustration.
X, an individual, opens a bank account using the mobile app or website of Y, a bank. To complete the Know-Your-Customer requirements under law for opening of bank account, X opts for processing of her personal data by Y in a live, video-based customer identification process. Y shall accompany or precede the request for the personal data with notice to X, describing the personal data and the purpose of its processing.

(2) Where a Data Principal has given her consent for the processing of her personal data before the date of commencement of this Act,—
(a) the Data Fiduciary shall, as soon as it is reasonably practicable, give to the Data Principal a notice informing her,––
(i) the personal data and the purpose for which the same has been processed;
(ii) the manner in which she may exercise her rights under sub-section (4) of section 6 and section 13; and
(iii) the manner in which the Data Principal may make a complaint to the Board, in such manner and as may be prescribed.
(b) the Data Fiduciary may continue to process the personal data until and unless the Data Principal withdraws her consent.

(3) The Data Fiduciary shall give the Data Principal the option to access the contents of the notice referred to in sub-sections (1) and (2) in English or any language specified in the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution.

3. Notice given by Data Fiduciary to Data Principal. —The notice given by the Data Fiduciary to the Data Principal shall—
(a) be presented and be understandable independently of any other information that has been, is or may be made available by such Data Fiduciary;
(b) give, in clear and plain language, a fair account of the details necessary to enable the Data Principal to give specific and informed consent for the processing of her personal data, which shall include, at the minimum, —
(i) an itemised description of such personal data; and
(ii) the specified purpose or purposes of, and specific description of the goods or services to be provided or uses to be enabled by, such processing; and
(c) give, the particular communication link for accessing the website or app, or both, of such Data Fiduciary, and a description of other means, if any, using which such Data Principal may—
(i) withdraw her consent, with the ease of doing so being comparable to that with which such consent was given;
(ii) exercise her rights under the Act; and
(iii) make a complaint to the Board.
tasks.simple_words: Section 5 sets the Act-level notice baseline. Rule 3 adds operational detail about independence of the notice, clear and plain language, itemised personal data, specified purpose, and the links or means for withdrawal, rights and complaints.
key_terms: information that accompanies or precedes a consent request under Section 5
purpose mentioned in the notice under the Act and Rules
individual to whom personal data relates
tasks.real_world_example: A bank's mobile onboarding flow requests video-based KYC data. The Act's illustration in Section 5 shows the request being accompanied or preceded by notice describing the personal data and purpose.
tasks.student_angle: A college scholarship portal asks for student identity information. The notice should be checked against the exact statutory and Rule 3 requirements rather than copied from a generic privacy policy.
common_mistakes: A notice can be understandable only by reading another document first.
Rule 3(a) says it shall be understandable independently of other information made available by the Data Fiduciary.
Rule 3 supplies the prescribed notice detail under the Act; both must be read together.

questions.prompt: Under Section 5(1), when must the notice be given?
options: Only after consent
Accompanying or preceding the request for consent
Only after a complaint
Only after processing ends
questions.why: Section 5(1) requires the notice to accompany or precede the consent request.
why_wrong: The notice is not postponed until after consent or processing.
A complaint is a separate mechanism.

questions.prompt: Which Rule 3 requirement concerns the notice's relationship to other information?
options: It must be understandable independently
It must be hidden behind a login
It must be verbal only
It must be provided after processing
questions.why: Rule 3(a) states that the notice shall be understandable independently of other information made or made available by the Data Fiduciary.
why_wrong: The other options are not Rule 3(a).

questions.prompt: A consent notice lists the data but does not state the specified purpose or specific description of the service/use. Which provision should be checked?
options: Rule 3(b)(ii)
Section 15
Section 18
Rule 20
questions.why: Rule 3(b)(ii) requires the specified purpose or purposes and a specific description of goods, services or uses enabled.
why_wrong: The other provisions do not contain this notice requirement.

questions.prompt: Rule 3(c) addresses means for withdrawal of consent, exercising rights and making a complaint to the Board.
options: True
False
questions.why: Rule 3(c)(i)-(iii) lists all three.
why_wrong: False contradicts the text.

questions.prompt: Fill the flag with the Rule that prescribes notice requirements.
options: DPDP{rule_3}
DPDP{rule_6}
DPDP{rule_10}
DPDP{rule_14}
questions.why: Rule 3 is the notice provision.
why_wrong: Rules 6, 10 and 14 address different subjects.

tasks.title: Task 2: Consent
official_text:
6. (1) The consent given by the Data Principal shall be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous with a clear affirmative action, and shall signify an agreement to the processing of her personal data for the specified purpose and be limited to such personal data as is necessary for such specified purpose.

Illustration.
X, an individual, downloads Y, a telemedicine app. Y requests the consent of X for (i) the processing of her personal data for making available telemedicine services, and (ii) accessing her mobile phone contact list, and X signifies her consent to both. Since phone contact list is not necessary for making available telemedicine services, her consent shall be limited to the processing of her personal data for making available telemedicine services.

(2) Any part of consent referred in sub-section (1) which constitutes an infringement of the provisions of this Act or the rules made thereunder or any other law for the time being in force shall be invalid to the extent of such infringement.

Illustration.
X, an individual, buys an insurance policy using the mobile app or website of Y, an insurer. She gives to Y her consent for (i) the processing of her personal data by Y for the purpose of issuing the policy, and (ii) waiving her right to file a complaint to the Data Protection Board of India. Part (ii) of the consent, relating to waiver of her right to file a complaint, shall be invalid.

(3) Every request for consent under the provisions of this Act or the rules made thereunder shall be presented to the Data Principal in a clear and plain language, giving her the option to access such request in English or any language specified in the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution and providing the contact details of a Data Protection Officer, where applicable, or of any other person authorised by the Data Fiduciary to respond to any communication from the Data Principal for the purpose of exercise of her rights under the provisions of this Act.

(4) Where consent given by the Data Principal is the basis of processing of personal data, such Data Principal shall have the right to withdraw her consent at any time, with the ease of doing so being comparable to the ease with which such consent was given.

(5) The consequences of the withdrawal referred to in sub-section (4) shall be borne by the Data Principal, and such withdrawal shall not affect the legality of processing of the personal data based on consent before its withdrawal.

(6) If a Data Principal withdraws her consent to the processing of personal data under sub-section (5), the Data Fiduciary shall, within a reasonable time, cease and cause its Data Processors to cease processing the personal data of such Data Principal unless such processing without her consent is required or authorised under the provisions of this Act or the rules made thereunder or any other law for the time being in force in India.

(7) The Data Principal may give, manage, review or withdraw her consent to the Data Fiduciary through a Consent Manager.

(8) The Consent Manager shall be accountable to the Data Principal and shall act on her behalf in such manner and subject to such obligations as may be prescribed.

(9) Every Consent Manager shall be registered with the Board in such manner and subject to such technical, operational, financial and other conditions as may be prescribed.

(10) Where a consent given by the Data Principal is the basis of processing of personal data and a question arises in this regard in a proceeding, the Data Fiduciary shall be obliged to prove that a notice was given by her to the Data Principal and consent was given by such Data Principal to the Data Fiduciary in accordance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder.
tasks.simple_words: Consent has statutory quality requirements and must be tied to the specified purpose and necessary personal data. Withdrawal is possible at any time when consent is the basis, and the Data Fiduciary has the evidentiary burden described in Section 6(10) when the question arises in a proceeding.
key_terms: free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous with clear affirmative action
tasks.real_world_example: A telemedicine app asks for treatment-related data and separately requests access to a phone contact list. The statutory illustration says consent is limited to personal data necessary for the specified telemedicine purpose.
tasks.student_angle: An online exam platform asks for consent to process exam data and separately asks for unrelated contact-list access. Students can use Section 6(1) to test whether the extra data is necessary for the specified purpose.
common_mistakes: Consent can waive any statutory right if the user clicks accept.
Section 6(2) makes an infringing part invalid to the extent of the infringement.
Withdrawal must always be harder than giving consent.

questions.prompt: Which word is NOT among the qualities expressly listed for consent in Section 6(1)?
options: Free
Specific
Informed
Secret
questions.why: Section 6(1) lists free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, with clear affirmative action.
why_wrong: Free, specific and informed are expressly listed.
Secret is not one of the listed statutory qualities.

questions.prompt: Section 6(4) gives a Data Principal what right when consent is the basis of processing?
options: A right to withdraw consent at any time
A right to appoint the Board
A right to impose a penalty
A right to change the Act
questions.why: Section 6(4) expressly provides the right to withdraw consent at any time, subject to the stated ease requirement.
why_wrong: The other options are not rights granted by Section 6(4).

questions.prompt: A service makes withdrawal of consent substantially harder than giving consent. Which statutory requirement is directly relevant?
options: Comparable ease of withdrawal
Board composition
Penalty schedule
Appellate Tribunal procedure
questions.why: Section 6(4) requires the ease of withdrawal to be comparable to the ease with which consent was given.
why_wrong: The other options concern unrelated provisions.

questions.prompt: Under Section 6(10), where the consent question arises in a proceeding, the Data Fiduciary has the burden described in that subsection.
options: True
False
questions.why: Section 6(10) expressly places that obligation on the Data Fiduciary.
why_wrong: False contradicts the text.

questions.prompt: Fill the flag with the section governing consent.
options: DPDP{section_6}
DPDP{section_5}
DPDP{section_8}
DPDP{section_13}
questions.why: Section 6 is titled Consent.
why_wrong: Sections 5, 8 and 13 cover notice, fiduciary obligations and grievance redressal respectively.

rooms.summary: Section 5 and Rule 3 establish the notice layer. Section 6 establishes consent requirements, withdrawal and Consent Manager provisions. Read the exact text before applying any example.
cheat_sheet: Section 5: notice accompanies or precedes consent request.
Rule 3: independent, clear and plain notice with specified details and access means.
Section 6(1): free, specific, informed, unconditional, unambiguous, clear affirmative action.
Section 6(4): withdrawal at any time with comparable ease.
Section 6(10): Data Fiduciary bears the stated proof obligation when the consent question arises in a proceeding.

final_challenge.scenario: A telemedicine app asks for treatment-related data and unrelated contact-list access, then provides a difficult withdrawal flow. Identify the two statutory concepts that must be checked first.
final_challenge.answer_explanation: Section 6 addresses necessary personal data for the specified purpose and comparable ease of withdrawal; Rule 3 also addresses notice and withdrawal means.

tasks.simple_words: This room explains Data Processor Obligations using the cited Act provision and any expressly linked notified Rule. The platform separates statutory requirements from practical examples.
